text: react-window is a component library that helps render large lists of data quickly and without the performance problems that often go along with rendering a lot of data. It's used in a lot of places, from React DevTools to the Replay browser. If you've never used a library like this before, you may want to read the how it works section first. Installation Begin by installing the library from NPM: TypeScript definitions are included within the published dist folder. Support Here are some ways to support this project: Become a GitHub sponsor Buy me a coffee
title: Getting started with react-window

headings.title: Can I attach a ref to the top-level HTMLDivElement?
headings.text: Can I attach a ref to the top-level HTMLDivElement? Although there is no prop exposed to do this directly, you can use a callback ref for this.

headings.title: Can Grid cells be auto-sized?
headings.text: Can Grid cells be auto-sized? No. Grid cell sizes must be known ahead of time- either because they are static or because they can be derived (from the data in CellProps) without needing to be rendered.

text: The ARIA grid role can be used to identify an element that contains one or more rows of cells. The Grid component automatically adds this role to the root HTMLDivElement it renders, but because individual cells are rendered by your code- you must assign ARIA attributes to those elements. To simplify this, the recommended ARIA attributes are passed to the cellComponent in the form of the ariaAttributes prop. The easiest way to use them is just to pass them through like so:
title: ARIA roles

text: Use the Grid component to render data with many rows and columns: Grids require you to specify the number of rows and columns as well as the width and height of each: Column widths and row heights can be either numbers or functions. In the example above, row height is fixed and column width is a function that determines the width of the column based on the column index: Lastly grids require a component to render a cell, given a column and row index. As with lists, this component receives additional props specified as part of cellProps: Grids require space to render cells. Typically the ResizeObserver API is used to determine how much space there is available within the parent DOM element. If an explicit width and height are specified (in pixels) using the style prop, ResizeObserver will not be used.

headings.title: scrollToCell
headings.text:
scrollToCell Scrolls the grid so that the specified row and column are visible.
Like the browser's scrollIntoView, items are aligned within the CSS scroll-padding of the element being scrolled
(e.g. scroll-padding-top can leave room for a sticky header).
 
 behavior Determines whether scrolling is instant or animates smoothly
 columnAlign Determines the horizontal alignment of the element within the grid
 columnIndex Index of the column to scroll to (0-based)
 rowAlign Determines the vertical alignment of the element within the grid
 rowIndex Index of the row to scroll to (0-based)

headings.title: scrollToColumn
headings.text:
scrollToColumn Scrolls the grid so that the specified column is visible.
Like the browser's scrollIntoView, items are aligned within the CSS scroll-padding of the element being scrolled
(e.g. scroll-padding-top can leave room for a sticky header).
 
 align Determines the horizontal alignment of the element within the grid
 behavior Determines whether scrolling is instant or animates smoothly
 index Index of the column to scroll to (0-based)

headings.title: scrollToRow
headings.text:
scrollToRow Scrolls the grid so that the specified row is visible.
Like the browser's scrollIntoView, items are aligned within the CSS scroll-padding of the element being scrolled
(e.g. scroll-padding-top can leave room for a sticky header).
 
 align Determines the vertical alignment of the element within the grid
 behavior Determines whether scrolling is instant or animates smoothly
 index Index of the row to scroll to (0-based)

headings.title: Hooks
headings.text: Hooks The useGridRef hook returns a mutable ref object. And the useGridCallbackRef hook returns a ref callback function. This is better when sharing the ref with another hook or component.

text:
Ref used to interact with this component's imperative API.
This API has imperative methods for scrolling and a getter for the outermost DOM element.
 The useGridRef and useGridCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.
title: GridImperativeAPI

headings.title: cellComponent
headings.text:
React component responsible for rendering a cell.
 This component will receive columnIndex, rowIndex, and style props by default.
Additionally it will receive prop values passed to cellProps.
 The prop types for this component are exported as CellComponentProps

headings.title: cellProps
headings.text:
Additional props to be passed to the cell-rendering component.
Grid will automatically re-render cells when values in this object change.
 This object must not contain ariaAttributes, columnIndex, rowIndex, or style props.

headings.title: columnCount
headings.text: Number of columns to be rendered in the grid.

headings.title: columnWidth
headings.text:
Column width; the following formats are supported:

number of pixels (number)
percentage of the grid's current width (string)
function that returns the column width (in pixels) given an index and cellProps 

 Percentage widths can't be resolved during server rendering unless a defaultWidth (or a pixel width via the style prop) is specified.

headings.title: rowCount
headings.text: Number of rows to be rendered in the grid.

headings.title: rowHeight
headings.text:
Row height; the following formats are supported:

number of pixels (number)
percentage of the grid's current height (string)
function that returns the row height (in pixels) given an index and cellProps 

 Percentage heights can't be resolved during server rendering unless a defaultHeight (or a pixel height via the style prop) is specified.

headings.title: children
headings.text:
Additional content to be rendered within the grid (above cells).
This property can be used to render things like overlays or tooltips.

headings.title: className
headings.text: CSS class name.

headings.title: columnKey
headings.text:
Grids use the column index as a key by default.
This prop can be used along with the rowKey prop to provide a custom key value.
 Custom keys can ensure better UX for sortable or filterable grids,
particularly if your cell components are stateful.
Refer to the React documentation for more info.
 This prop cannot be auto-memoized because it is called during render.
It is important to always useCallback for this prop; do not use an inline function.

headings.title: defaultHeight
headings.text:
Default height of grid (in pixels) for initial render, before its actual height has been measured.
 Grids can't be measured during server rendering, so this value determines how many rows are server rendered.
It's recommended to set this to the expected height of the grid (or to specify a pixel height via the style prop).

headings.title: defaultScrollLeft
headings.text:
Initial horizontal scroll offset (in pixels) of the grid.
This value is only applied once, when the grid first mounts with at least one column.
 Server-rendered HTML can't be pre-scrolled, so server rendering always starts at the first column;
the default scroll offset is applied once the grid hydrates.
 If the grid can't be scrolled that far when the offset is applied (e.g. it is hidden with display: none,
or uses percentage column widths before its width has been measured), the offset is clamped or ignored and not retried.
Specify a defaultWidth (or a pixel width via the style prop) when using percentage column widths.

headings.title: defaultScrollTop
headings.text:
Initial vertical scroll offset (in pixels) of the grid.
This value is only applied once, when the grid first mounts with at least one row.
 Server-rendered HTML can't be pre-scrolled, so server rendering always starts at the first row;
the default scroll offset is applied once the grid hydrates.
 If the grid can't be scrolled that far when the offset is applied (e.g. it is hidden with display: none,
or uses percentage row heights before its height has been measured), the offset is clamped or ignored and not retried.
Specify a defaultHeight (or a pixel height via the style prop) when using percentage row heights.

headings.title: defaultWidth
headings.text:
Default width of grid (in pixels) for initial render, before its actual width has been measured.
 Grids can't be measured during server rendering, so this value determines how many columns are server rendered.
It's recommended to set this to the expected width of the grid (or to specify a pixel width via the style prop).

headings.title: dir
headings.text:
Indicates the directionality of grid cells.
 The directionality of an ancestor element can't be detected during server rendering;
specify this prop explicitly for server-rendered right-to-left grids.
 See HTML dir global attribute for more information.

headings.title: gridRef
headings.text:
Imperative Grid API.
 The useGridRef and useGridCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.

headings.title: onCellsRendered
headings.text: Callback notified when the range of rendered cells changes.

headings.title: onResize
headings.text:
Callback notified when the Grid's outermost HTMLElement resizes.
This may be used to (re)scroll a cell into view.

headings.title: overscanCount
headings.text:
How many additional rows/columns to render outside of the visible area.
This can reduce visual flickering near the edges of a grid when scrolling.

headings.title: rowKey
headings.text:
Grids use the row index as a key by default.
This prop can be used along with the columnKey prop to provide a custom key value.
 Custom keys can ensure better UX for sortable or filterable grids,
particularly if your cell components are stateful.
Refer to the React documentation for more info.
 This prop cannot be auto-memoized because it is called during render.
It is important to always useCallback for this prop; do not use an inline function.

headings.title: scrollElement
headings.text:
Element that scrolls the grid, for grids that scroll along with other content (e.g. the page):

"window" to scroll with the page
an ancestor element that scrolls (e.g. stored with a useState ref callback); null until it has mounted

 The grid renders at its full height and only renders the rows (and columns) visible within the scroll element's viewport.
Its position within the scroll element is measured whenever it renders, scrolls, or resizes,
and whenever content before it is resized, inserted, or removed (e.g. an image loading above the grid).

columns scroll with the scroll element too if the grid is as wide as its content (e.g. style={{ width: "max-content" }});
otherwise the grid fills the width of its parent and its columns scroll within it
 scrollToCell, scrollToColumn and scrollToRow scroll whichever element scrolls each axis
 defaultHeight and defaultWidth are used as the viewport size until the scroll element has been measured (e.g. during server rendering)
percentage row heights and column widths are relative to the scroll element's viewport
 defaultScrollLeft and defaultScrollTop are ignored

 While the scroll element is null, the grid renders the first rows (as it does during server rendering).
 The grid's onScroll handler is only called when the grid scrolls its own columns;
listen to the scroll element's "scroll" events instead (or use the useIsScrolling hook).

headings.title: style
headings.text:
Optional CSS properties.
The grid of cells will fill the height and width defined by this style.

headings.title: tagName
headings.text:
Can be used to override the root HTML element rendered by the Grid component.
The default value is "div", meaning that Grid renders an HTMLDivElement as its root.
 In most use cases the default ARIA roles are sufficient and this prop is not needed.

text:
Renders data with many rows and columns.
 Unlike List rows, Grid cell sizes must be known ahead of time.
Either static sizes or something that can be derived (from the data in CellProps) without rendering.
title: Grid component props

text: Grids can also display right to left languages (like Arabic). The grid components check the dir attribute to determine content directionality. Using the same data as from the previous example, here is a grid rendered right to left.
title: Right to left content

text: Grid provides an imperative API for responding to events. The recommended way to access this API is to use the exported ref hook: Attach the ref during render: And call API methods in an event handler: The form below uses the imperative API to scroll the grid: Align Scroll behavior Job title Column Scroll The Grid API also provides scrollToColumn and scrollToRow methods for single-axis scrolling. Note If you are passing the ref to another component or hook, use the ref callback function instead.
title: Imperative methods

headings.title: Parameters
headings.text: Parameters target : "window" | HTMLElement | null | undefined The element that scrolls: a list or grid's own element (e.g. from useListCallbackRef) "window" or the scroll element, for lists and grids that use the scrollElement prop options ?: { delay?: number } = {} delay: milliseconds without scroll events after which scrolling is considered to have ended; defaults to 150. Scrolling ends when the browser fires a scrollend event. The delay is only used by browsers that don't support that event.

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value isScrolling : boolean Whether the target is currently scrolling. Scrolling that starts and ends before React renders (e.g. an instant scroll) may not change this value. Changing this value re-renders any rows it is passed to (e.g. via rowProps) when scrolling starts and when it ends.

text: The useIsScrolling hook tracks whether a list (or grid) is scrolling. Rows can use this value to render simplified content while scrolling, in place of content that is expensive to render. Click below for examples of how to use the hook. Scrolling a list Scrolling with the window
title: useIsScrolling

text: In most cases, the useIsScrolling hook should be passed a reference to the list HTMLElement. In the contacts list below, each row renders an avatar, a name, and a job title. While the list is scrolling, rows render lightweight placeholders instead:
title: Tracking list scrolling with useIsScrolling

text: For lists that scroll with the page, pass the string "window" instead of the list's element:
title: Tracking window scrolling with useIsScrolling

headings.title: Parameters
headings.text: Parameters count : number Number of items. defaultScrollOffset ?: number = 0 Initial scroll offset (in pixels), applied once when the element first mounts with at least one item. Ignored when a scrollElement is specified. defaultSize ?: number = 0 Size (in pixels) of the viewport before it has been measured (e.g. during server rendering); this determines how many items are initially rendered. dir ?: "ltr" | "rtl" Direction of horizontal content; detected from the element (or its ancestors) by default. direction ?: "horizontal" | "vertical" = "vertical" Direction that items are laid out in. element : HTMLElement | null Element that scrolls the items or, if a scrollElement is specified, the element that contains the items. Item offsets are relative to the start of this element's content. itemSize : number | string | ((index: number) => number) | DynamicRowHeight Item size; the following formats are supported: number of pixels (number) percentage of the viewport's size (string) function that returns the item size (in pixels) given an index dynamic row height cache returned by the useDynamicRowHeight hook (vertical only); rendered items must be passed to measureElement and specify a data-index attribute Sizes are cached until the value of this option changes; memoize functions (e.g. with useCallback) and only change them when sizes change. onItemsRendered ?: (visibleItems: { startIndex: number; stopIndex: number }, allItems: { startIndex: number; stopIndex: number }) => void Callback notified when the range of visible (or rendered) items changes. overscanCount ?: number = 3 How many additional items to render outside of the visible area. scrollElement ?: "window" | HTMLElement | null Element that scrolls the items, for items that scroll along with other content (e.g. the page): "window" to scroll with the page, or an ancestor element that scrolls (null until it has mounted). See the scrolling with the page page for more information.

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value items : { index: number; offset: number; size: number }[] Items to render (including overscan). Offsets are relative to the start of the element's content; sizes are estimates for dynamic sizes that have not yet been measured. measureElement : (element: Element | null) => void Ref callback for rendered items, required for items with dynamic sizes (see itemSize). scrollToIndex : ({ align, behavior, index }) => void Scrolls the element (or scroll element) so that the specified item is visible. Like the browser's scrollIntoView, items are aligned within the CSS scroll-padding of the element being scrolled (e.g. scroll-padding-top can leave room for a sticky header). totalSize : number Total size (in pixels) of all items; an estimate for dynamic sizes that have not yet been measured. visibleRange : { startIndex: number; stopIndex: number } Range of items within the visible area (excluding overscan).

text: The List and Grid components render their own markup. To render custom markup instead (e.g. a <table>), use the useVirtualizer hook. It calculates which items to render and where; how they are rendered is up to you. Click below for examples of how to use the hook. Rendering a list Rendering a table Rendering items with dynamic heights
title: useVirtualizer

text: Items with dynamic row heights (like the messages in the chat log below) must be passed to the measureElement ref callback and specify a data-index attribute:
title: Rendering items with dynamic heights with useVirtualizer

text: The useVirtualizer hook returns the items to render (each with an index, offset, and size) along with the totalSize of all items. Items can be absolutely positioned within an element of that size: Refer to the useVirtualizer page for the full list of parameters and return values.
title: Rendering a list with useVirtualizer

text: Rows in a <table> can't be absolutely positioned. Instead, rows can be rendered in normal document flow, with spacer rows taking the place of rows that aren't rendered. Using the <tbody> as the element (and the scrolling container as the scrollElement) positions rows relative to the body, so the sticky header doesn't offset them: Like the browser's scrollIntoView, scrollToIndex aligns items within the scroll-padding of the element being scrolled. Setting scroll-padding-top to the height of the sticky header keeps rows from being aligned underneath it. The aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex attributes tell assistive technologies how many rows the table has, even though only some of them are rendered.
title: Rendering a table with useVirtualizer

text: Libraries like this help to render a lot of items as efficiently as possible by limiting how many items are rendered at once. Here is an over-simplified illustration of a list with 6 columns. Only 3 or 4 columns are rendered at a time because that is enough to fill the viewport. (The user can't see the other columns, so we don't need to render them). 1 2 3 4 5 6 When a user scrolls the list, a different set of columns are rendered- but always only a few at a time. The illustration above shows unrendered columns as dimmed. In reality, they aren't there at all. The columns that do get rendered are positioned using CSS properties like left to mimic other columns before them. To render one of these items, all you need to provide is a component like the one below.
title: How does it work?

text: Lists that load their data as the user scrolls can use the onRowsRendered callback to decide when to load more. For example, a feed can load the next page when the user scrolls near the end. Scroll the activity feed below to load more updates: Loading state prevents the same page from being requested more than once while the user scrolls.
title: Infinite loading

text: The ARIA list role can be used to identify a list of items. The List component automatically adds this role to the root HTMLDivElement it renders, but because individual rows are rendered by your code- you must assign ARIA attributes to those elements. To simplify this, the recommended ARIA attributes are passed to the rowComponent in the form of the ariaAttributes prop. The easiest way to use them is just to pass them through like so:
title: ARIA roles

text: Sometimes the height of a row isn't known until it's been rendered. For example, a chat log with messages of varying length. For this kind of list, react-window provides a helper hook called useDynamicRowHeight. In this case, rows can just render their content as they normally would and react-window will measure it for you. Dynamic row heights are not as efficient as predetermined sizes. It's recommended to provide your own height values if they can be determined ahead of time. Dynamic-height lists scroll to the target row instantly, even when smooth scrolling is requested.
title: Dynamic row heights

text: The simplest type of list to render is one with fixed row heights. To render this type of list, you need to specify how many rows it contains (rowCount), which component should render rows (rowComponent), and the height of each row (rowHeight): The rowProps object can also be used to share data between components. Values passed in rowProps will also be passed as props to the row component: Lists require vertical space to render rows. Typically the ResizeObserver API is used to determine how much space there is available within the parent DOM element. If an explicit height is specified (in pixels) using the style prop, ResizeObserver will not be used.
title: Fixed row heights

text: Images are an example of dynamic row heights. As with text, the useDynamicRowHeight hook can be used to measure images. If the dimensions of each image are known ahead of time, pass them to the as width and height attributes. The browser will reserve space for the image before it loads, so rows are measured at the correct size right away (rather than resizing once the image arrives). A placeholder can be rendered behind the image while it loads.
title: Images

headings.title: anchorRow
headings.text:
anchorRow Keeps the specified row where it is on screen through changes in row heights, e.g. when the user expands or collapses it.
Call this before making the change.
By default, the list keeps the first visible row that didn't change height in place,
so a row at the top of the viewport that grows would extend upward (its top edge would move out of view).
 Ignored if the row isn't visible when row heights change; only applies to dynamic row heights.
 
 duration How long (in milliseconds) to keep the row in place; defaults to 1000
 index Index of the row to keep in place (0-based)

headings.title: scrollToRow
headings.text:
scrollToRow Scrolls the list so that the specified row is visible.
Like the browser's scrollIntoView, items are aligned within the CSS scroll-padding of the element being scrolled
(e.g. scroll-padding-top can leave room for a sticky header).
Dynamic row heights are measured after rendering;
Content that resizes later may require another scrollToRow call.
 For dynamic height lists, "smooth" scrolling is animated by the list (rather than the browser)
so that the destination can be corrected as rows are measured along the way.
 
 align Determines the vertical alignment of the element within the list
 behavior Determines whether scrolling is instant or animates smoothly
 index Index of the row to scroll to (0-based)

headings.title: Hooks
headings.text: Hooks The useListRef hook returns a mutable ref object. And the useListCallbackRef hook returns a ref callback function. This is better when sharing the ref with another hook or component.

text:
Imperative List API.
 The useListRef and useListCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.
title: ListImperativeAPI

text: Chat logs and other streaming content often keep the list scrolled to the bottom as new rows arrive, unless the user has scrolled up to read older content. Reset demo chat This example builds on dynamic row heights. Each time a row is added the list smoothly scrolls to the bottom, as long as the user hasn't scrolled away from it. Rows are measured as scrollToRow scrolls past them, so the list keeps correcting its destination until the last row is in view.
title: Pinned to bottom

headings.title: rowComponent
headings.text:
React component responsible for rendering a row.
 This component will receive an index and style prop by default.
Additionally it will receive prop values passed to rowProps.
 Spread ariaAttributes onto the row element; they identify it as a row (e.g. so that dynamic row heights are measured reliably)
 The prop types for this component are exported as RowComponentProps

headings.title: rowCount
headings.text: Number of items to be rendered in the list.

headings.title: rowHeight
headings.text:
Row height; the following formats are supported:

number of pixels (number)
percentage of the list's current height (string)
function that returns the row height (in pixels) given an index and rowProps 
dynamic row height cache returned by the useDynamicRowHeight hook

 Percentage heights can't be resolved during server rendering unless a defaultHeight (or a pixel height via the style prop) is specified.
 With dynamic row heights, the list keeps the rows on screen in place when rows above them change height
(e.g. as they are measured while scrolling up, or when their content resizes) by adjusting the scroll position.
The rows kept in place are those after the first visible row that didn't change height,
so rows revealed by scrolling up move out of the way as they're measured.
To keep a specific row in place instead (e.g. one the user is expanding), call anchorRow before changing it.
The scroll position is not adjusted while the list is scrolled to the end (e.g. a chat pinned to the bottom)
or while scrollToRow is scrolling to a row.
 Dynamic row heights are not as efficient as predetermined sizes.
It's recommended to provide your own height values if they can be determined ahead of time.

headings.title: rowProps
headings.text:
Additional props to be passed to the row-rendering component.
List will automatically re-render rows when values in this object change.
 This object must not contain ariaAttributes, index, or style props.

headings.title: children
headings.text:
Additional content to be rendered within the list (above rows).
This property can be used to render things like overlays or tooltips.

headings.title: className
headings.text: CSS class name.

headings.title: defaultHeight
headings.text:
Default height of list (in pixels) for initial render, before its actual height has been measured.
 Lists can't be measured during server rendering, so this value determines how many rows are server rendered.
It's recommended to set this to the expected height of the list (or to specify a pixel height via the style prop).

headings.title: defaultScrollOffset
headings.text:
Initial scroll offset (in pixels) of the list.
This value is only applied once, when the list first mounts with at least one row.
 Server-rendered HTML can't be pre-scrolled, so server rendering always starts at the first row;
the default scroll offset is applied once the list hydrates.
 If the list can't be scrolled that far when the offset is applied (e.g. it is hidden with display: none,
or uses percentage row heights before its height has been measured), the offset is clamped or ignored and not retried.
Specify a defaultHeight (or a pixel height via the style prop) when using percentage row heights.

headings.title: listRef
headings.text:
Ref used to interact with this component's imperative API.
 This API has imperative methods for scrolling and a getter for the outermost DOM element.
 The useListRef and useListCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.

headings.title: onResize
headings.text:
Callback notified when the List's outermost HTMLElement resizes.
This may be used to (re)scroll a row into view.

headings.title: onRowsRendered
headings.text: Callback notified when the range of visible rows changes.

headings.title: overscanCount
headings.text:
How many additional rows to render outside of the visible area.
This can reduce visual flickering near the edges of a list when scrolling.

headings.title: rowKey
headings.text:
Lists use the row index as a key by default.
This prop can provide a custom key value.
 Custom keys can ensure better UX for sortable or filterable lists,
particularly if your row components are stateful.
Refer to the React documentation for more info.
 With dynamic row heights (see useDynamicRowHeight), measured heights are stored by key,
and the rows on screen are kept in place when rows are inserted or removed above them
(e.g. when older messages are loaded at the top of a chat),
so don't adjust the scroll position yourself after inserting rows.
 This function is called for many rows (e.g. to calculate row positions), so it should be cheap,
like reading an id: (index, { items }) => items[index].id.
Keys must be stable: a row's key must not change when other rows are inserted or removed,
so don't use the index or a random value.
 This prop cannot be auto-memoized because it is called during render.
It is important to always useCallback for this prop; do not use an inline function.

headings.title: scrollElement
headings.text:
Element that scrolls the list, for lists that scroll along with other content (e.g. the page):

"window" to scroll with the page
an ancestor element that scrolls (e.g. stored with a useState ref callback); null until it has mounted

 The list renders at its full height and only renders the rows visible within the scroll element's viewport.
Its position within the scroll element is measured whenever it renders, scrolls, or resizes,
and whenever content before it is resized, inserted, or removed (e.g. an image loading above the list).

 scrollToRow scrolls the scroll element
 defaultHeight is used as the viewport height until the scroll element has been measured (e.g. during server rendering)
percentage row heights are relative to the scroll element's viewport height
 defaultScrollOffset is ignored

 While the scroll element is null, the list renders the first rows (as it does during server rendering).
 The list itself doesn't scroll, so its onScroll handler isn't called;
listen to the scroll element's "scroll" events instead (or use the useIsScrolling hook).

headings.title: style
headings.text:
Optional CSS properties.
The list of rows will fill the height defined by this style.

headings.title: tagName
headings.text:
Can be used to override the root HTML element rendered by the List component.
The default value is "div", meaning that List renders an HTMLDivElement as its root.
 In most use cases the default ARIA roles are sufficient and this prop is not needed.

text: Renders data with many rows.
title: List component props

text: By default, lists and grids scroll their own content. To scroll a list along with the rest of the page instead (e.g. a feed), pass "window" as the scrollElement prop: The list renders at its full height and only renders the rows that are visible within the viewport. Its position on the page is measured whenever it renders, scrolls, or resizes, and whenever content before it is resized, inserted, or removed (e.g. an image loading above it). A list can also scroll along with other content inside of a scrollable element. Pass the element as the scrollElement prop (it will be null until it has mounted). For example, the activity feed below scrolls along with the content above and below it: The imperative API scrolls the scroll element, and sticky rows stick to the top of the scroll element. Grids support this prop too. Rows scroll with the scroll element; columns also scroll with it if the grid is as wide as its content. Otherwise the grid fills the width of its parent and its columns scroll within it. When a scroll element is provided: defaultHeight (and defaultWidth for grids) are used as the viewport size until the scroll element has been measured (e.g. during server rendering) Percentage row heights (and column widths) are relative to the scroll element's viewport Default scroll offsets are ignored; the list doesn't control the scroll element's position
title: Scrolling with the page

text: List provides an imperative API for responding to events. The recommended way to access this API is to use the exported ref hook: Attach the ref during render: And call API methods in an event handler: The form below uses the imperative API to scroll the list: Align Scroll behavior State Scroll Note If you are passing the ref to another component or hook, use the ref callback function instead.

text: If you want to render content on top of your list or grid, the safest method is to use a portal and render them directly into the parent document. This avoids potential clipping issues or z-index conflicts. For the specific case of "sticky" rows, you can render within the parent list or grid using the children prop. For example, the leaderboard below keeps your own ranking pinned to the top while the list scrolls: The example above was created using code like this: Note the height of 0 in the example above prevents the sticky row from affecting the height of the parent list.

State "header" rows are taller and are styled differently. This list requires a rowHeight function that tells it what height a row should be based on the type of data it contains.
title: Variable row heights

text: This library requires React version 18 or newer. It also uses the ResizeObserver (or a polyfill) to calculate the available space for List and Grid components. ResizeObserver usage can be avoided if explicit pixel dimensions are specified using the style prop. (Percentage or EM/REM based dimensions do not count.)
title: Requirements

headings.title: Sizing
headings.text: Sizing Lists and grids normally measure their available space using a ResizeObserver, but there is nothing to measure on the server. Instead, use the defaultHeight prop (and defaultWidth prop for grids) to tell react-window how much space to fill. This determines how many rows (and columns) are server rendered. Alternatively, specify an explicit pixel size using the style prop (e.g. style={{ height: 400 }}). This size is used on both the server and the client, so no measurement is needed at all. Without a default size, only the first row (and any overscan rows) will be server rendered. Once the page hydrates, the list will measure itself and render the remaining rows. Percentage-based sizes (e.g. rowHeight="25%") can't be resolved without a size. Unless a default size (or a pixel size via the style prop) is specified, they are server rendered with a size of 0 and rows will overlap until the page hydrates. The default size only determines how many rows are rendered before the list has been measured; the list's actual size is still determined by CSS. To server render more rows than are visible (e.g. for crawlers that don't run JavaScript), set defaultHeight to a value larger than the list's height. The extra rows will be removed once the page hydrates, but keep in mind that hydration cost grows with the number of rows rendered.

headings.title: Right to left content
headings.text: Right to left content Grids inherit their direction from ancestor elements, but this can't be detected on the server. Specify the dir prop explicitly for server-rendered right-to-left grids.

headings.title: Scrollbar size
headings.text: Scrollbar size getScrollbarSize returns 0 on the server. To avoid hydration mismatches, read it after the component has mounted (e.g. within an effect) instead of during render. Click below for more guidance about server rendering. Server rendering with React Server Components Server rendering with dynamic row heights Server rendering with an initial scroll position

text: List and Grid can be rendered on the server (including static site generation and React Server Components). Server-rendered rows are visible before JavaScript has loaded, and they hydrate without mismatches.
title: Server rendering

text: Rows with dynamic heights can't be measured until they are rendered in a browser. Until then, server-rendered rows are displayed in normal document flow (rather than being positioned using estimated heights) so that they don't overlap or leave gaps. Once the page hydrates and rows have been measured, they are positioned as usual. To reduce layout shift once rows have been measured, per-row heights can be provided to useDynamicRowHeight using the initialRowHeights option. These heights are used in place of the default height until rows are measured. For example, they might be estimated from each row's content: Heights can also be measured ahead of time, e.g. by rendering the list in a headless browser while generating a static site. When rendering from a Server Component, compute the heights on the server and pass them as a prop to the client component that calls useDynamicRowHeight. If row heights can be determined exactly ahead of time, use a rowHeight function instead; it's more efficient than measuring rows. Initial heights are matched to rows by index, and dynamic heights often depend on the list's width (e.g. text that wraps). Heights that were computed for different data or a different width will cause layout shift once rows are measured. Changing the hook's key option re-reads initialRowHeights.
title: Server rendering with dynamic row heights

text: Use the defaultScrollOffset prop (or the defaultScrollLeft and defaultScrollTop props for grids) to set the initial scroll position. HTML can't be pre-scrolled, so the server always renders the first rows of the list. The default scroll offset is applied once the page hydrates (or, for lists that are initially empty, once they have rows), unless the list has already been scrolled (e.g. by the browser restoring a previous scroll position).
title: Server rendering with an initial scroll position

text: List and Grid are client components, but they can be rendered directly by a Server Component as long as all of their props can be sent from the server to the client: The rowComponent (or cellComponent) must be a client component, marked with the "use client" directive. Values in rowProps (or cellProps) must be serializable. Functions can't be passed from the server to the client, so props like rowHeight functions, rowKey, onRowsRendered, onResize, and listRef (as well as hooks like useDynamicRowHeight) need to be used within a client component:
title: Server rendering with React Server Components

text: GitHub is the easiest place to look for help, but it's probably not the fastest. This project is maintained by a single developer so there is limited bandwidth for answering questions. I recommend asking questions on Stack Overflow or Reddit to start with. Both sites have active communities who often respond quickly. If you don't find an answer there you can try opening a GitHub issue- but please take a moment first to see if your question has has already been answered before opening a new one.
